title: Only 32% of GCs Are Meeting Their AI Goals. Here's Why Preconstruction Is the Fix.
summary: Autodesk's 2026 data shows 68% of GCs haven't met their AI goals. Here's why preconstruction is where purpose-built AI actually delivers ROI.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


- Autodesk's 2026 State of AI in Construction report found that only 32% of the construction leaders it surveyed, general contractors among them, have met their AI goals.
- The failure pattern is consistent: GCs deploy generic AI tools on the wrong workflows and expect results.
- Preconstruction is where AI delivers the clearest, fastest ROI. The document volume is high. The manual work is measurable. The cost of errors is real.
- Purpose-built tools like[Scope Agent](https://provision.com/scope-agent) and[Risk Review](https://provision.com/risk-review) are built for pre-con workflows. Generic AI is not.
- The fix is not more AI. It is the right AI on the right problem.


Sixty-eight percent of construction leaders deployed AI and did not get what they expected. That is the finding buried in Autodesk's 2026 State of AI in Construction report. Only 32% said they met their AI goals.


If you are a VP of Pre-Construction or Chief Estimator reading that number, it probably does not surprise you. You have seen the demos. You have heard the pitches. You may have even run a pilot that went nowhere.


But here is the thing: the problem is not AI. The problem is where and how construction firms are deploying it.


Preconstruction is the one area where AI has a documented, measurable case for ROI. Firms that deploy purpose-built tools on pre-con workflows are not in the 68% club. This article explains why.


## Why Most Construction AI Deployments Fail


Generic AI tools are built for general knowledge work. They summarize documents, draft emails, and answer broad questions. They were not built to read a 2,000-page project specification, cross-reference it against 400 drawing sheets, and produce a trade-by-trade scope package.


When GCs use general-purpose AI for construction document work, they run into the same wall every time:


- No understanding of spec division structure or drawing sheet hierarchies
- No ability to cross-reference drawings against specs without manual setup
- No handling of addenda without restarting the entire process
- No structured output that an estimator can actually hand to a sub
- No citations back to the exact clause, section, or drawing sheet


These are not edge cases. They are the core of pre-con document work. And generic AI cannot do any of them reliably.


So when a GC deploys Copilot or ChatGPT on bid documents and gets inconsistent results, they write off "AI" as a category. That is the wrong conclusion. They deployed the wrong tool.


## What Makes Preconstruction Different


Pre-con is not like project delivery. The document volume is concentrated. A single pursuit can involve thousands of pages of drawings, specifications, contracts, addenda, and RFIs. All of it needs to be read, cross-referenced, and acted on in days, not weeks.


The manual work is also quantifiable. A single bid requires 30–40 hours of estimator time just to build a scope-of-work package. Contract and spec review adds another layer. For[general contractors](https://provision.com/general-contractors) running 20, 30, or 50 pursuits a year, the math compounds fast.


And the cost of getting it wrong is documented. According to the Arcadis Global Construction Disputes Report, the average North American construction dispute in 2024 was worth $60.1 million. Errors and omissions in contract documents have repeatedly ranked as the number one dispute cause in North America.


That is the environment preconstruction teams operate in. High document volume, tight timelines, real financial consequences for errors, and not enough people to cover it all manually.


AI built for this environment does not look like a chatbot. It looks like a system that can ingest a full project set, understand the relationships between documents, and produce structured outputs that are actually usable on bid day.


## The Scope Gap Problem Is Not Random


One of the clearest signals of a pre-con process failure is a scope gap that shows up after award. A line item nobody priced. A trade boundary nobody defined. Work the sub says is not in their number.


These gaps are not random. They follow a predictable pattern. The[Scope Gap Playbook](https://provision.com/ebooks/scope-gap-playbook) , built from 200+ interviews with GC preconstruction teams across North America, found that the same habits produce the same gaps, project after project.


The most common anti-pattern: writing "as per plans and specs" in a scope sheet and moving on. That phrase does not define scope. It defers the conflict to later, usually after the sub has already underbid and is looking for a way out.


As one Pre-Construction Lead at a Top-ENR Canadian GC put it: "It's descriptive: bread, put it on a plate, use the open jar. You have to get to that level of detail or else they'll just be like, 'you didn't tell us that.'"


The dollar examples from the playbook tell the same story:


- A $200K wood-flooring scope gap on a luxury condo project, missed because the scope sheet referenced drawings that conflicted with the finish schedule
- A $300K lead-lined glass omission on a hospital imaging suite, absorbed by the GC under "readily inferable" language
- A $400K missed roof cover board on a $50M project, recovered only through a relational concession from the sub


None of these were typos. They were systematic failures in the scope-writing process. And they are exactly the kind of problem that purpose-built AI is designed to catch before bid day.


## Where Purpose-Built AI Actually Delivers


The gap between "AI tools we bought" and "AI goals we met" is a capability gap. Construction AI needs to do things that general AI simply does not.


Here is where purpose-built tools are delivering measurable results for[GC preconstruction teams](https://provision.com/general-contractors) in 2026:

In internal validation, Scope Agent achieves 97% match accuracy on scope item extraction. The human estimator baseline on the same exercise is 91.3%, at roughly four days per project. That gap is not about replacing estimators. It is about giving them a better starting point.

Provision's[Risk Review](https://provision.com/risk-review) runs a risk checklist across contracts and specs with 99% accuracy on risk identification. Every risk is cited to the exact clause, section, or page. It delivers an 80% reduction in contract and spec review time.


Compare that to the five-minutes-before-bid review that happens on most pursuits. That is not a process. That is hoping nothing gets missed.

The Arcadis data on $60.1M dispute values exists for a reason. Contract risk that is not caught before award does not go away. It becomes a dispute.


### Document Q&A on the Full Project Set

The alternative is an estimator spending 20 minutes hunting through a 1,400-page spec book for a single detail. Multiply that by the number of questions per pursuit and by the number of pursuits per year. The time cost is not trivial.


Provision has processed 66,000 documents and answered more than 50,000 queries across $100 billion in project value. Those are not pilot numbers.


## The Architecture Argument: Why Generic AI Cannot Close This Gap


The Autodesk 2026 report does not just surface a stat. It surfaces a structural problem. Generic AI is being deployed on workflows it was not designed for, and construction leaders are absorbing the disappointment as a signal that AI does not work.


The architecture of a purpose-built construction AI is fundamentally different from a general-purpose model:


Capability Generic AI (ChatGPT, Copilot) Purpose-Built Construction AI (Provision)


Full project-set ingestion (drawings + specs + contracts) No Yes


Cross-reference drawings against specifications No Yes


Addenda handling without restarting No Yes


Structured trade-by-trade scope output No Yes


Citation to exact clause, section, or page Inconsistent Yes, every time


Risk flagged to contract language No Yes


These are not feature differences. They are capability differences. A tool that cannot read drawings cannot help you catch a scope gap between the civil drawings and the architectural finish schedule. No prompt engineering fixes that.


## What the 32% Are Doing Differently


The firms meeting their AI goals in 2026 are not necessarily running the most sophisticated technology stacks. They are applying AI to the right problems with the right tools.


The pattern across the GCs seeing results:


1. **They started in pre-con, not project delivery.** Pre-con has discrete, document-heavy tasks. The scope of success is clear. You either produced a scope package or you did not. That makes ROI easier to measure and faster to prove.
2. **They used purpose-built tools, not general ones.** The firms seeing results are not running spec reviews through ChatGPT. They are using tools that were designed to read construction documents and produce construction outputs.
3. **They picked a single high-value workflow and proved it.** Scope packages. Contract review. Spec search. One clear use case with a measurable before-and-after. Then they expanded.
4. **They measured hours saved, not impressions of the tool.** An estimator saving 25 hours per bid on a team running 40 pursuits a year is 1,000 hours recovered. That is real. Saying "our team is more efficient" is not.


The[NAC case study](https://provision.com/case-studies-nac) and the[Cleveland Construction case study](https://provision.com/case-studies-cleveland-construction) both follow this pattern: specific workflow, specific tool, specific result.


## The Preconstruction Case Is Not Theoretical


The 2018 PlanGrid and FMI study "Construction Disconnected" found that miscommunication and bad project data drove $31.3 billion in U.S. rework costs. That figure is from 2018. The document complexity has only increased since then.


Pre-con is where bad data enters the project. A scope sheet that says "as per plans and specs" does not define work. It defers a future argument. A risk clause nobody flagged before execution becomes a dispute after. A missed trade boundary on bid day becomes a change order in the field.


As one Estimating Manager at a Canadian ICI GC said during research for the Scope Gap Playbook: "We have less subs who just kind of a gentleman's agreement. They've become more quick to clarify that we're not including that one piece of scope."


The margin pressure is real. The sub behavior is real. The document volume is real. AI that was built to handle this environment can help. AI that was not built for it will add noise, not signal.


If your firm is in the 68% that has not met its AI goals, the first question is not "should we invest more in AI?" The first question is: "Are we deploying AI on the right workflow with the right tool?"

### Why are only 32% of GCs meeting their AI goals in 2026?


Autodesk's 2026 State of AI in Construction report reports this figure across the construction leaders it surveyed, general contractors among them. Generic tools lack the ability to read drawings, cross-reference full project sets, handle addenda, and produce structured trade-by-trade outputs. Without those capabilities, results are inconsistent and ROI is hard to prove.

Pre-con has concentrated, document-heavy tasks with clear outputs: scope packages, contract reviews, spec searches.
